citations.narrative:
The facility is not keeping records of births or hatchings. There were no records of acquisition for the birth of two goats or
the hatching of six rheas.
Improper recordkeeping does not allow APHIS officials to properly account for animals on the premises or allow for proper
tracking of animals. Every dealer shall make, keep, and maintain records or forms which fully and correctly disclose all
information required by the AWA concerning animals purchased or otherwise acquired, owned, held, leased, or otherwise
in his or her possession or under his or her control, or which is transported, sold, euthanized, or otherwise disposed of by
that dealer or exhibitor. The records shall include any offspring born or hatched of any animal while in his or her
possession or under his or her control, to the extent that any identification or counting of offspring can be carried out
without unduly disturbing nesting or rearing activities.
To be corrected by November 6, 2026.

There are two nonhuman primate enclosures with evidence of excessive rust.
In the enclosure housing one black spider monkey, the top of a metal barrel is rusted through. This has created a large,
jagged hole with pieces of broken metal that the primate can access. In the enclosure housing three patas monkeys, one
of the metal structures has at least two areas of excessive rust where the surface has rusted through completely. This has
created holes with rusted, jagged edges where the primates can access them.
Rust can compromise structural strength, present roughened or broken surfaces where it is possible for the nonhuman
primates to injure themselves, and prevent proper cleaning and sanitization of a surface. Any surfaces that come in
contact with the nonhuman primates must be free of excessive rust that prevents the required cleaning and sanitization,
or that affects the structural strength of the surface.
To be corrected by November 20, 2026.

There are two areas of the perimeter fence with large gaps between the bottom of the fence and the ground, leaving the
black spider monkey, the patas monkeys, the ring-tailed lemurs, the vervets, and the snow macaques without an
adequate perimeter fence. One of the gaps measures 7 inches high and extends approximately 21 inches across.
Gaps under the perimeter fence can allow unwanted animals to gain access to the facility and potentially harm the
animals within. The perimeter fence must be constructed so that it protects nonhuman primates by restricting
unauthorized humans, and animals the size of dogs, skunks, and raccoons from going through it or under it and having
contact with the nonhuman primates.

The tower section of the primary enclosure for the ring-tailed lemurs is not being kept in good repair. Near the top of the
tower, the wooden platform is showing signs of deterioration with broken edges. The is also a wooden board with a screw
head sticking out at least an inch from the surface.
Nonhuman primate primary enclosures that are not in good repair can lead to injury. Primary enclosures must be
designed and constructed of suitable materials so that they are structurally sound for the species of nonhuman primates
contained in them. They must be kept in good repair.
To be corrected by November 20, 2026.

There are two areas of the perimeter fence with large gaps between the bottom of the fence and the ground, leaving the
Patagonian cavies without an adequate perimeter fence. One of the gaps measures 7 inches high and extends
approximately 21 inches across.
Gaps under the perimeter fence can allow unwanted animals to gain access to the facility and potentially harm the
animals within. A perimeter fence with gaps is also not able to act as secondary containment for the animals and can lead
to escape. The perimeter fence must be constructed so that it protects the animals in the facility by restricting animals and
unauthorized persons from going through it or under it and having contact with the animals in the facility, and so that it can
function as a secondary containment system for the animals in the facility.

The enclosure housing one yellow-naped amazon contains rust that affects the structural integrity of the surface of
multiple support poles. On one of the horizontal support poles that the bird perches on, there are five holes where the
surface has rusted through completely. The facility has attempted to mitigate the rust by spraying a coating on other poles
in the enclosure; however, many of these poles show signs of pitting and flaking rust coming through the coating.
Rust can compromise the structural integrity of surfaces, create rough and jagged areas that could injure the birds, and
prevent proper cleaning and sanitization, increasing the risk of contamination and disease. Interior surfaces and surfaces
that come in contact with birds must be free of rust or damage that affects the structural integrity of the surface or
prevents cleaning.
To be corrected by November 20, 2026.

The items inside the primary enclosure for one yellow-naped amazon are not being maintained in a way that protects the
bird from injury. There are two plastic baskets hanging from the enclosure that show signs of chewing from the bird. The
edge of the lower basket is broken all the way around and the basket contains broken fragments of plastic.
Plastic items that are easily damaged by the animal can result in injury or illness from ingestion. Primary enclosures must
be constructed and maintained so that they protect the birds from injury.
To be corrected by November 6, 2026.

The facility is not providing a pool or aquatic area in the primary enclosure housing three geese.
Failure to provide a pool or aquatic area prevents these birds from exhibiting their normal, species-specific behaviors and
can lead to poor condition, debility, stress, and abnormal behavioral patterns. Primary enclosures housing wading and
aquatic birds must contain a pool or other aquatic areas (e.g., ponds, waterfalls, fountains, and other water features) and
a dry area that allows easy ingress or egress of the pool or other aquatic area. Pools and other aquatic areas must be of
sufficient surface area and depth to allow each bird to make normal postural and social adjustments, such as immersion,
bathing, swimming, and foraging, with adequate freedom of movement and freedom to escape from aggression
demonstrated by other birds in the enclosure.
To be corrected by November, 6, 2026.

citations.desc: Cleaning, sanitization, housekeeping, and pest control.
citations.narrative:
The facility is not sanitizing the food receptacles for birds as often as necessary. The food bowl for one yellow-naped
amazon has a build-up of dark brown material with whitish specks on the inside surface. Fresh food had been placed in
the food bowl that morning by staff.
Failure to sanitize food receptacles as often as necessary can lead a build-up of debris and grime that can contaminate
food and lead to illness in the bird. Primary enclosures and food and water receptacles for birds must be sanitized as
often as necessary to prevent accumulation of dirt, debris, food waste, excreta, and other disease hazards.
To be corrected by November 6, 2026.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with facility representatives.
You may appeal all or part of any inspection report by submitting a written statement contesting the findings—along with
any supporting documentation—to the Deputy Administrator. Appeals of routine, focused, or attempted inspections must
be received within 21 days of report issuance as shown by the signature line of this report.
Appeals may be sent by email to AnimalCare@usda.gov.
Appeals sent by mail should be addressed to:

APHIS Animal Care (AC)
U.S. Department of Agriculture

Mailstop #3W11
